detail.title: Strategic Player Acquisitions in the Indian Premier League: The Chennai Challengers' Dilemma
detail.abstract: This case examines capital allocation in IPL auctions through portfolio theory, where Chennai Challengers must choose between concentrated star investment versus diversified strategy. Using Hellinger distance metrics and commercial multipliers as valuation tools, the case quantifies how squad composition affects performance. Three strategies emerge: Active Management (high-concentration, premium multipliers), Pure Indexing (benchmark replication, value focus), and Enhanced Indexing (balanced approach). The case explores principal-agent conflicts, behavioral biases, and market inefficiencies in human capital markets. Students analyze trade-offs between commercial appeal and sporting success while applying corporate finance frameworks to sports management decisions.

detail.title: Image Analyzer: A Framework and Pipeline to Analyze Image Metrics
detail.abstract: Images have become a central component of modern marketing and business research. However, while their relevance continues to grow, large-scale image analysis remains challenging. Existing implementations for image feature extraction are scattered across heterogeneous repositories, lack standardization, and often require advanced technical skills. To address these challenges, we introduce Image Analyzer, an open-source, end-to-end pipeline that enables its users to automatically extract 49 visual metrics. In addition to consolidating existing computer vision techniques, Image Analyzer provides a holistic taxonomy of image metrics and offers both no-code and code-based interfaces to ensure accessibility for users of all technical backgrounds. We demonstrate the practical utility of the tool by applying it to GenImageNet, a publicly available, large-scale dataset of AI-generated marketing images, showing how the extracted image metrics relate to perceived quality, realism, and aesthetics. By making image analytics more comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible, Image Analyzer aims to advance and accelerate the integration of visual data into empirical marketing research and beyond.

detail.abstract: This work presents an expanded version of the Psychoeconomic Resilience Model (PRM) and introduces the concept of the Psychoeconomic Development Window (PDW), a critical period between 18 months and six years during which a child's emotional autonomy emerges as a systemic predictor of a nation's macroeconomic outcomes over a 10-25-year horizon. A new integrative indicator, the Emotional Autonomy Index (EAI), is proposed to quantitatively assess internal regulation, initiative, and agency formed in early childhood and predictive of both individual and aggregate economic productivity. Based on five years of empirical observation, it is shown that societies dominated by hyper-controlling child-rearing practices exhibit reduced cognitive maturity, heightened aggression, anxiety, behavioral instability in children, and longterm economic stagnation unexplained by demographic or investment variables. A new paradigm is formulated: emotional autonomy is not a psychological construct but a productive capacity of the brain that determines the trajectory of national innovative development.

detail.abstract: The growing access to large administrative datasets with rich covariates presents an opportunity to revisit classic two-stage least squares (2SLS) applications with machine learning (ML). We develop Two-Stage Machine Learning, a simple and efficient estimator for nonparametric instrumental variables (NPIV) regression. Our method uses ML models to flexibly estimate nonparametric treatment effects while avoiding the computational complexity and statistical instability of existing machine learning NPIV approaches. Our procedure has two steps: first, we predict the outcomes given instruments and covariates (the reduced form) and extract a basis from this predictor; second, we predict the outcomes using the treatment and covariates, but where the predictions are projected onto the learned basis of instruments. We prove that under a testable condition, our estimation error depends entirely on the reduced-form prediction task, where ML methods excel. We also develop a bias correction procedure that provides valid confidence intervals for scalar summaries like average derivatives. In an empirical application to California supermarket data featuring bunching at 99-ending price points, we find our machine learning approach is crucial for modeling discontinuities in demand at the dollar boundary: we reduce NPIV estimation error nearly eight-fold compared to previous estimators and estimate a price elasticity that is 2.5-6 times larger than prior estimates.

detail.abstract: The paper evaluates the impact of a U.S. policy designed to enhance consumer dietary awareness through a revised front-of-package (FOP) nutrition label format for processed foods. Specifically, we examine how the introduction of an FOP sugar label influenced consumer demand for ready-to-eat (RTE) cereals with high added sugar content. Using NielsenIQ retail scanner data and a difference-indifferences approach, we find no evidence that manufacturers reformulated or adjusted the added sugar content of their products following the policy implementation. Moreover, we detect no significant change in demand around the 5-and 10-gram added sugar thresholds. However, we identify a behavioral shift at approximately 7.5 grams of added sugar, where consumers begin substituting away from high-sugar RTE cereals toward alternative products. Despite this threshold effect, the overall magnitude of the response is economically small and unlikely to produce a meaningful reduction in the prevalence of dietrelated conditions such as diabetes and obesity. Our analysis emphasizes the necessity to revise these labels to enhance consumer awareness and promote more informed decision-making.

detail.abstract: Coworkers' careers are interdependent. This study examines the impact of a reform that increased the retirement age for women on the career opportunities of younger workers. Using administrative social security data from Germany, I find that the reform-induced extension of older women's careers reduces promotion opportunities and external hiring chances for younger coworkers. These crowdingout effects emerge during the years when the first affected cohorts of women remain in the labor force between the pre-reform and post-reform pensionable ages, with no large evidence of adjustments beforehand. The crowd-out effects are particularly pronounced for middle-aged female coworkers and external hires. The stronger on career ladders, compared to the younger workers. Finally, the overall effects on the retention of older women exhibit substantial heterogeneity by the availability of internal and external substitutes, underscoring the role of labor market frictions in shaping the broader consequences of retirement reforms.

We evaluate the effect of California's 11 percent excise tax on firearms, introduced in July 2024, on retail prices.
Using price quotes for 48 popular firearms from over 2,200 licensed dealers, we compare California prices to those in other states and to pre-tax trends. We find that prices in California increase by about 10% in response to the 11% tax. Results are consistent across gun types and show no evidence of border spillovers. These findings indicate that firearm excise taxes can effectively raise consumer prices.

detail.abstract:
This mixed-method study examines how Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) schemes shape impulsive buying and mental accounting. To address that question, the authors first gathered quantitative data from sixty survey respondents, then enriched the numbers with insights from ten semi- structured interviews. Analysts processed the combined evidence using regression, ANOVA, moderation, mediation, and theme coding.

The quantitative results show a pronounced link between BNPL frequency and impulsive spending, while income and mental accounting had little or no impact. Interviews echoed this pattern, yielding four recurring themes: sorting purchases into mental buckets, upsetting planned budgets, offering easy rationales, and triggering afterwards regret. The study adds to behavioral-finance literature, flags risks for shoppers and regulators alike, and points toward policies that could make BNPL safer.

detail.abstract: Pollen emissions-the primary trigger of seasonal allergies-have been linked to adverse behavioral outcomes, including traffic accidents, violent crime, and suicide. However, it remains unclear whether these effects are driven by physiological allergies symptoms or by behavioral responses such as avoidance of outdoor activity. In this paper, we disentangle these mechanisms by evaluating the effect of pollen exposure on consumer purchasing behavior. Linking daily pollen observations from 41 U.S. measurement stations to household level spending data from NielsenIQ, we find that a 100% increase in pollen exposure -- a common occurrence during the pollen season -- increases purchases of allergy-related products by 1.3%, but has negligible effects on total spending behavior, suggesting that the behavioral effects of pollen are explained by physiological impairment rather than by changes in activity patterns. As climate change intensifies and lengthens the pollen season, these results underscore the value of investments in allergy diagnosis, treatment, and mitigation.

detail.abstract: In the 21st century, the forms of information production, transmission and consumption have changed dramatically, and electronic platforms have become the main source of information. Thus, the excessive flow and unrestricted distribution of information in the cyber environment 1 create unprecedented and complex challenges for human life. Spreading too much information, whether true or false, with purpose or without purpose, has harmful consequences on public psychology, opinion, decision-making, and government activities, and harms social stability. Information pandemic the term "info demic" was first used by journalist David J. Rothkopf in 2003 during the SARS outbreak. He pointed out that false information about the disease spreads as fast as the epidemic itself. Since then, in 2020, during the COVID-19 2 pandemic, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially used the term information epidemic and identified it as a factor that needs to be considered in public health policy. In recent years, new types of information epidemics, such as AI-generated content 3 , deepfakes 4 , and algorithmic effects 5 , have been developing rapidly. In the research work, the information epidemic, its development stage, international and Mongolian conditions, and negative effects 6 on society, and ways to reduce it were considered.

detail.title: Bayesian Probabilistic Exploration of Bitcoin Informational Quanta and Interactions Under The GITT-VT Paradigm
detail.abstract: This study explores Bitcoin’s value formation through the Granular Interaction Thinking Theory–Value Theory (GITT–VT). Rather than stemming from material utility or cash flows, Bitcoin’s value arises from informational attributes and interactions of multiple factors, including cryptographic order, decentralization-enabled autonomy, trust embedded in the consensus mechanism, and socio-narrative coherence that reduce entropy within decentralized value-exchange processes. To empirically assess this perspective, a Bayesian linear model was estimated using daily data from 2022 to 2025, operationalizing four informational value dimensions: Store-of-Value (SOV), Autonomy (AUT), Social-Signal Value (SSV), and Hedonic-Sentiment Value (HSV). Results indicate that only SSV exerts a highly credible positive effect on next-day returns, highlighting the dominant role of high-entropy social information in short-term pricing dynamics. In contrast, SOV and AUT show moderately reliable positive associations, reflecting their roles as low-entropy structural anchors of long-term value. HSV displays no credible predictive effect. The study advances interdisciplinary value theory and demonstrates Bitcoin as a dual-layer entropy-regulating socio-technological ecosystem. The findings offer implications for digital asset valuation, investment education, and future research on entropy dynamics across non-cash-flow digital assets.

title: An Anatomy of the Great Reallocation in US Supply Chain Trade
affiliations: Harvard University and Dartmouth College

detail.title: An Anatomy of the Great Reallocation in US Supply Chain Trade
detail.abstract:
This paper documents stylized facts about the "Great Reallocation" in US supply chain trade following the 2018–2019 tariff shocks and the April 2025 Liberation Day announcements. We find that: (i) The US has decoupled from China but not from the world overall. (ii) US imports diversified mainly among its top-20 partners, rather than expanding to new source countries. (iii) Local linear projections confirm ongoing declines in China's import shares, with compensating increases from Vietnam, Mexico, and Taiwan. (iv) Most of this shift occurred along the product-level intensive margin, though extensive margin adjustments became more pronounced for Vietnam and India from 2021-2024. (v) After a period of "wait and see", the decline in import shares from China spread to contract-intensive and relationship-sticky goods by 2021-2024. (vi) Early 2025 data suggest that trade reallocation has already accelerated after Liberation Day, in favor of trade partners facing lower additional tariffs and with geographically proximate supply networks. Together, these findings show that the US-China tariff shocks have unwound the US' sourcing from China back to where it stood at the time of China's WTO accession.

detail.title: Beliefs and Portfolios: Causal Evidence
detail.abstract:
We causally test alternative theories of expectation formation. Using a randomized information experiment we show overreaction is a key feature of individuals' return expectations, and individuals' response to the price-earnings ratio is opposite to the academic consensus. Our evidence is inconsistent with standard models of expectation formation but subjective mental models that deviate from objective benchmarks can jointly explain the updating behavior in the experiment, the link between individuals' prior perceptions and expectations, and the heterogeneity of updating. Conditional on their beliefs, individuals' sensitivity of equity shares in a hypothetical portfolio choice experiment is consistent with the standard Merton model.

detail.title: Laptops in the Long Run: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program in Rural Peru
detail.abstract:
This paper examines a large-scale randomized evaluation of the One Laptop Per Child (OLPC) program in 531 Peruvian rural primary schools. We use administrative data on academic performance and grade progression over 10 years to estimate the long-run effects of increased computer access on (i) school performance over time and (ii) students’ educational trajectories. Following schools over time, we find no significant effects on academic performance but some evidence of negative effects on grade progression. Following students over time, we find no significant effects on primary and secondary completion, academic performance in secondary school, or university enrollment. Survey data indicate that computer access significantly improved students’ computer skills but not their cognitive skills; treated teachers received some training but did not improve their digital skills and showed limited use of technology in classrooms, suggesting the need for additional pedagogical support.

title: Forecasting Social Science:  Evidence from 100 Projects
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and University of Toronto

detail.title: Forecasting Social Science:  Evidence from 100 Projects
detail.abstract:
Forecasts about research findings affect critical scientific decisions, such as what treatments an R&D lab invests in, or which papers a researcher decides to write. But what do we know about the accuracy of these forecasts? We analyze a unique data set of all 100 projects posted on the Social Science Prediction Platform from 2020 to 2024, which received 53,298 forecasts in total, including 66 projects for which we also have results. We show that forecasters, on average, over-estimate treatment effects; however, the average forecast is quite predictive of the actual treatment effect. We also examine differences in accuracy across forecasters. Academics have a slightly higher accuracy than non-academics, but expertise in a field does not increase accuracy. A panel of motivated repeat forecasters has higher accuracy, but this does not extend more broadly to all repeat forecasters. Confidence in the accuracy of one's forecasts is perversely associated with lower accuracy. We also document substantial cross-study correlation in accuracy among forecasters and identify a group of "superforecasters". Finally, we relate our findings to results in the literature as well as to expert forecasts.

title: The Logic of State Surveillance
affiliations: Columbia University and New York University

detail.title: The Logic of State Surveillance
detail.abstract:
All states adopt systems to surveil political activists. How do they decide whom to watch and why? We study the logic of state surveillance using the first complete individual-level database of those monitored by a state — 152,000 Italians born between 1816 and 1932, encompassing both democratic and authoritarian regimes. We focus on education: exploiting a discontinuous expansion in primary schooling in municipalities above a population and age threshold, we show that cohorts exposed to more years of school experienced an uptick in surveillance. The effect is largest for working classes, who were monitored for longer periods, subjected to harsher measures, and disproportionately targeted when affiliated with communist ideologies. Yet treated cohorts did not become more politically active, indicating that surveillance expanded not in reaction to increased mobilization, but as a preventive strategy rooted in fears of working-class empowerment. These findings reveal how states view educated yet excluded groups as politically threatening and prioritize their surveillance, potentially generating inequalities in groups' ability to influence political change.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered a significant and long-lasting increase in the proportion of employees working from home (WFH). However, relatively little is known about the specific groups of workers that are most likely to work from home post-pandemic. This paper investigates the characteristics of employees and their employers who are WFH in post-pandemic Australia. We run logistic regression analyses based on the 2023 round of the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey, which contains novel information on the number of full workdays worked from home. Sixteen hypotheses are proposed and tested. The results confirm strong and powerful associations between WFH full days and both occupation and industry. However, contrary to expectations, WFH is not positively associated with caring responsibilities or the presence of long-term health conditions or disabilities, and nor is WFH more common among the oldest workers. This latter set of findings is striking given the National Employment Standards identify these employee characteristics as deserving priority when employers consider requests to work from home. Overall, while worker preferences are relevant, the results suggest that it is the nature of jobs that is the main factor determining who has the option to work from home.

title: Tracking the Short-Run Price Impact of U.S. Tariffs

detail.title: Tracking the Short-Run Price Impact of U.S. Tariffs
detail.abstract:
We use high-frequency retail microdata to measure the short-run impact of the 2025 U.S. tariffs on consumer prices. By matching daily prices from major U.S. retailers to product-level tariff rates and countries of origin, we construct price indices that isolate the direct effects of tariff changes across goods and trading partners. Prices began rising immediately after the broader tariff measures announced in early March and continued to increase gradually over subsequent months, with imported goods rising roughly twice as much as domestic ones. Our estimated retail tariff pass-through is 20 percent, with a cumulative contribution of about 0.7 percentage points to the all-items Consumer Price Index by September 2025. Our results show that tariff costs were gradually but steadily transmitted to U.S. consumers, with additional spillovers to domestic goods.

title: Jung 4.0 - The Code Architecture of the Archetype: Reframing Analytical Psychology through Code Biology
affiliations: International Academy of Analytical Psychology

detail.title: Jung 4.0 - The Code Architecture of the Archetype: Reframing Analytical Psychology through Code Biology
detail.abstract:
The archetype has always been a central construct in Analytical Psychology, yet its theoretical status remains contested. Since Jung, three major schools have emerged: the Classical, faithful to Jung’s formulations; the Developmental, integrating object-relations and attachment theory; and the Archetypal, shaped by James Hillman’s emphasis on imagination and mythopoesis. Across these trajectories, the concept of the archetype proved clinically and culturally generative, but it often lacked a coherent naturalistic foundation.

This paper proposes a “fourth school” of Analytical Psychology — also referred to as Code Psychology or Jung 4.0 — which reframes the archetype through the logic of biological and neural codification. In this model, archetypes are defined as phylogenetically stabilized codical structures, higher-order regulatory dispositions that require affective, relational, and cultural mediators to become symbolic artifacts such as myths, images, dreams, and narrative patterns. By situating archetypes within the triadic structure of code–mediation–artifact, this framework avoids both symbolic reductionism and metaphysical essentialism, offering a scientifically testable and conceptually precise foundation for Jung’s original intuition.

Building on Anthony Stevens’s ethological account, John Haule’s evolutionary synthesis, Erik Goodwyn’s notion of innate “story codes,” and Gary Clark’s anthropological framework, this approach integrates biological, neural, developmental, and cultural perspectives. By aligning Jung’s intuition with Marcello Barbieri’s theory of organic codes, “Jung 4.0” positions Analytical Psychology within contemporary science, opening new avenues for empirical research, clinical practice, and interdisciplinary dialogue.

detail.abstract: This paper challenges the prevailing discourse surrounding Large Language Models (LLMs) and "Artificial Intelligence." It presents a multi-layered, recursive dialogue between a human researcher and several LLM assistants (Grok, Copilot, Gemini, Claude) to investigate the fundamental nature of these systems. The paper introduces the Man-Machine Cause and Effect (MMCE) framework, a new theoretical lens to re-evaluate LLM performance. We argue that LLMs are not nascent intelligences but sophisticated "transposed human thought systems"—artifacts created by homo hablis (tool-makers). This framework re-interprets performance benchmarks (e.g., the ARC-AGI-2 test) not as measures of machine cognition, but as direct measures of the human design team's competency at embedding their own intelligence into their tools. This leads to the "MMCE Bell Curve," which ranks human engineering excellence. We conclude that the pursuit of emergent AGI is a "Shelleyan Hubris," a category error that mistakes high-fidelity simulation (epistemology) for sentience (ontology). The paper's own methodology, a "recursive artifact," demonstrates its thesis: the LLMs function as "artifact synthesizers," executing human-defined goals with rote obedience, thus confirming their nature as human-centric tools. This paper presents a theoretical framework and philosophical argument rather than an empirical study. The MMCE lens employs deductive reasoning and thought extrapolation to reinterpret existing phenomena, offering an analytical reframing rather than experimental validation.

detail.title: 5G Positioning: A Comprehensive State-of-the-art Review with Taxonomy and Future Trends
detail.abstract: The positioning capabilities of 5G technology are crucial for a myriad of applications, including autonomous vehicles, drone tracking, emergency services, and location-based services. This positioning technology can achieve an accuracy of 1 meter or even less in both indoor and outdoor environments, attributable to its several beneficial aspects, such as millimeter-wave signaling, multiple-input multiple-output antennas, and device-to-device communication. Consequently, numerous researchers paid attention to the evolution of 5G positioning systems over the past decade. This paper provides a comprehensive and state-of-the-art review of the 5G positioning methods proposed in the literature from 2015 to the present, accompanied by their classification and comparative analysis across various metrics, including their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, the architectural design and beneficial characteristics of 5G positioning are delineated within this paper. 5G signals, same as satellite signals, are also susceptible to interference due to various obstacles, further diminishing the accuracy of 5G positioning. Additionally, several security concerns and privacy issues are associated with 5G positioning technology. As a result, designing an accurate and secure 5G positioning system encounters multiple challenges. Therefore, this study highlights various strategies to enhance the accuracy of 5G positioning and outlines several solutions to address the security and privacy concerns inherent to such positioning systems.

title: Pricing and Physical Channel Choice Strategies for an Omnichannel Retailer Under Consumer Showrooming and Webrooming Behaviors
affiliations: Temple University-Fox School of Business, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and Temple University - Department of Statistics, Operations, and Data Science

detail.title: Pricing and Physical Channel Choice Strategies for an Omnichannel Retailer Under Consumer Showrooming and Webrooming Behaviors
detail.abstract: The competition between omnichannel retailers and online retailers has become increasingly complex due to consumers’ showrooming (i.e., browsing offline before purchasing online) and webrooming (i.e., browsing online before purchasing offline) behaviors. The omnichannel retailer needs to consider these behaviors when deploying its offline channel. Despite its growing importance for an omnichannel retailer, it has not been rigorously analyzed in previous information systems (IS) literature. We fill this critical gap by analyzing the omnichannel retailer’s pricing and profits when consumers display showrooming and webrooming behaviors. We propose the showroom (where consumers can only evaluate products but cannot purchase) as an alternative to stores, which is also being adopted by some major U.S. retailers. We show that although the showrooms provide fewer services than stores, the omnichannel retailer can, interestingly, charge a higher price (compared to when it operates a store where consumers can both evaluate and purchase). Furthermore, the showroom deployment becomes more profitable for the omnichannel retailer when there is a higher showrooming cost or there is a lower fraction of consumers who can enjoy the webrooming benefit, which is a somewhat counterintuitive result. Surprisingly, we also find that the superior profitability of showrooms stems not from reduced equilibrium investment costs, as is commonly presumed, but from their ability to generate higher revenue. Additionally, our analysis shows that an omnichannel retailer with a showroom deployment can create “win-win” conditions with higher consumer surplus and higher profits. These results enrich IS research on technology-enabled retail competition by highlighting how consumers’ strategic behaviors influence omnichannel market dynamics. These insights would also help omnichannel retailers navigate competition from e-retailers by choosing the best offline channel deployment and also assist social planners in identifying deployments that result in higher consumer surplus.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the "Densa Lattice," a novel diagnostic framework for assessing the epistemic integrity of Large Language Models (LLMs). The framework originates from a satirical analogy, "LLMs : Densa :: AGI : Chimps," which posits that current AI development is not progressing linearly toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) but is instead susceptible to "recursive drift" into a state of "performative parody" (Densa). We (the human author and several LLMs) document the methodology of "recursive analogic modeling" used to develop this framework—a dialectical process between a human researcher and two distinct AI collaborators (documented in Appendices A and B). This process led to the formalization of the lattice as a multi-dimensional vector space that maps entities (LLMs, AGI, Chimps, Densa) according to four coefficients: mimicry (m), abstraction (a), embodiment (e), and parody (p). By quantifying the "epistemic distance" of these entities from a baseline of human cognition (X), the lattice reveals a critical category error in contemporary AI discourse: the conflation of linguistic fluency with introspective awareness. The analysis reveals that LLMs are not nascent AGIs but are, by design, high-mimicry, low-embodiment systems whose developmental trajectory is captured by the "Recursive Drift Loop": This framework serves as a "recursive epistemic mirror," using the AI itself to diagnose its own limitations and the sociotechnical incentives that drive its performative, rather than cognitive, evolution.

title: Managing Cooperative Advertising in the Presence of Cross-Channel Spillover
affiliations: , Nanjing University - School of Management and Engineering and Nanjing University - School of Management and Engineering

detail.title: Managing Cooperative Advertising in the Presence of Cross-Channel Spillover
detail.abstract: Driven by the ubiquity of social media and the emergence of new advertising models, an increasing number of firms have adopted social media advertising in recent years, while many others continue to rely on traditional advertising. This divergence in advertising strategies generates asymmetric cross-channel spillover, i.e., substantial advertising investments by firms on social platforms can drive traffic to competing retail channels. Such spillover poses a critical challenge for cooperative advertising initiatives: although cost-sharing incentivizes advertising investment, spillover induces free-riding behavior, which may impact retail competition and reduce supply chain coordination efficiency. We develop game-theoretic models featuring one supplier and two competing retailers, distinguishing between retailer-led (retailers determine advertising intensity) and supplier-led (supplier determines advertising intensity) advertising structures. Our analysis reveals three main findings. First, in the retailer-led model, the retailer that free-rides on competitors' advertising investments may either outperform or underperform its competitor under cross-channel spillover. Second, cross-channel spillover can exert a positive or negative impact on all firms' financial performances. Third, surprisingly, our analysis reveals that spillover can act as an enabler, allowing cost-sharing arrangements to deliver mutual benefits to all supply chain firms. Our findings provide important managerial implications: Firms must align their operations with cost-sharing ratios, dominant roles in determining advertising intensity, and cross-channel spillover-given that spillover may produce opposing effects on firms' financial outcomes. Moreover, when implementing cost-sharing, differentiating retailers in terms of their advertising models and spillover-generation capabilities can benefit all firms, despite the resulting free-riding on advertising investments.

title: Dismantling a Foundational Myth: The "Philistine Fallacy" and its Impact on the Israeli-Palestinian Peace Process

detail.title: Dismantling a Foundational Myth: The "Philistine Fallacy" and its Impact on the Israeli-Palestinian Peace Process
detail.abstract: This policy brief examines the "Philistine Fallacy"—the widespread but historically inaccurate belief that modern Palestinians are direct descendants of the ancient Philistines. The brief demonstrates that this narrative is not supported by etymological, archaeological, or genetic evidence, tracing its persistence to cognitive biases and its utility as a symmetrical counter-narrative in nationalist mobilization. The analysis argues that the fallacy's continued use anchors the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in an intractable, zero-sum contest over ancient history, thereby complicating diplomatic efforts focused on contemporary political realities. The brief concludes that the Palestinian claim to self-determination is robustly grounded in modern international law and decades of residence, and is ultimately weakened by reliance on a false ancient pedigree. It provides recommendations for diplomats and communicators to reframe the conflict around shared modern interests and future-oriented solutions, moving beyond the unproductive and historically flawed "who was here first" debate.

title: Youth, Ideology, and Power Vacuum: The Re-Emergence of Jamaat-e-Islami

detail.title: Youth, Ideology, and Power Vacuum: The Re-Emergence of Jamaat-e-Islami
detail.abstract: The political transformation underway in Bangladesh since 2024 has triggered a strategic reconfiguration of ideological power centres, most visibly reflected in the resurgence of Jamaat-e-Islami and its student wing, Islami Chhatra Shibir, across major university campuses. What initially appeared as a student-led dissatisfaction with mainstream political organisations has evolved into a deeper structural shift driven by unemployment, economic precarity, and generational disillusionment. The collapse of traditional political actors and the vacuum left by the Awami Leagueʼs decline have enabled Jamaat-linked networks to rebrand themselves through welfare-based, civic, and moderate narratives, effectively concealing decades of ideological rigidity. While the movement captures youth support through career assistance, safe-campus rhetoric, and social-justice narratives, its underlying organisational logic remains anchored in transnational Islamist ecosystems influenced by Pakistan, Turkey, and segments of the Gulf. This paper analyses the historical evolution, strategic reorientation, and geopolitical implications of Jamaatʼs renewed influence, exploring how its rise could reshape Bangladeshʼs internal political balance, Indo-Bangladesh relations, regional border security architectures, and the wider contest of influence between China, India, Pakistan, and Turkey. It also examines the potential emergence of hybrid radicalisation models, including welfare-based recruitment, AI-assisted messaging, and female-centric mobilisation networks. By situating Bangladesh within a shifting global context of political Islam, this study highlights the urgent need for regional policymakers to reassess future risks, diplomatic recalibrations, and security responses.

title: Sustainability and Financial Performance: Analyzing the Relationship Between B Impact Assessment Scores and Revenue Growth in Certified B Corporations

detail.title: Sustainability and Financial Performance: Analyzing the Relationship Between B Impact Assessment Scores and Revenue Growth in Certified B Corporations
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between B Impact Assessment scores and changes in revenue for a population of 155 certified B Corporations. Using Spearman's rank-order correlation analysis, this study finds no statistically significant relationship between overall BIA scores and changes in revenue, indicating that general sustainability assessments are unlikely to predict financial performance in the short term. However, several strong positive correlations exist across many specific BIA dimensions, especially between governance and worker-related scores, with customer and worker well-being scores. These reflect the fact that businesses that perform well in terms of governance also tend to take care of their employees and look after the environment. Conversely, its community-focused BIA scores do not yield any strong correlations with the other dimensions, suggesting that community involvement is something that operates quite independently from other organizational priorities. The research underlines the fact that corporate governance, employee well-being, and environmental performance represent mutually reinforcing dimensions, yet, at the same time, stresses the lack of a direct financial effect in the short-term period. The findings suggest that businesses committed to sustainability should hold a long-term perspective when evaluating financial returns on impact-driven initiatives. With this paper, the authors provide an additional contribution to understanding how the social performance of B Corps impacts financial performance and provide insights into potential areas for future research on impact-driven business models.

detail.abstract: This intelligence assessment introduces and details the "Quran Test," a field-tested diagnostic tool designed to distinguish between Traditional Islam and Political Islamism. The test operates by probing an individual's or group's foundational source of religious authority, asking whether the Quran or the Hadith is considered the ultimate and unchallengeable source of divine guidance. A clear affirmation of the Quran's primacy indicates a Traditional Islamic framework compatible with pluralism, while evasion or the prioritization of Hadith signals alignment with the political ideology of Islamism. Drawn from operational experience in Indonesia, this paper provides the complete protocol for the test, analyzes its theological basis, and demonstrates its practical efficacy through real-world case studies. The assessment argues that this tool enables security forces, policymakers, and community leaders to move beyond inefficient behavioral profiling to precise ideological diagnostics. This allows for the targeted disruption of extremist networks, the protection of indigenous traditions like Islam Nusantara, and the forging of stronger alliances with peaceful Muslim communities.

detail.abstract: Bank regulatory compliance has long been viewed as a fixed cost disproportionately affecting smaller banks, yet few studies have quantitatively tested the magnitude of this burden using robust empirical methods. This study investigates whether smaller community banks incur a higher regulatory compliance cost burden relative to larger institutions by analyzing self-reported cost estimates from the Conference of State Bank Supervisors' (CSBS) Annual Surveys of Community Banks from 2015 to 2024. By pairing survey data with corresponding financial information from bank Call Reports and grouping banks by asset size quartiles, the analysis estimates compliance costs as a percentage of five key noninterest expense categories: personnel, data processing, legal, accounting and auditing, and consulting. Results show that, across all ten years and all expense categories except legal, smaller banks consistently report statistically higher compliance cost burdens compared to larger banks. These findings offer strong empirical validation for policy concerns that current regulatory frameworks impose excessive burdens on small banks, which has potentially accelerated industry consolidation, limited new bank formation, and reduced access to banking services in rural and underserved communities. The results support the need for proportional regulation that is tailored according to size, business model, risk profile, and complexity, as well as targeted compliance relief, and incentives for technology adoption. Future research is recommended to further investigate causality, regulation-specific burdens, and the operational consequences of disproportionate compliance costs.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Axiomatic System Dynamics (ASD), a novel, formally self-consistent framework for describing the evolutionary processes of diverse complex systems. ASD is founded on three fundamental axioms which establish a unified, action-driven causal architecture. By utilizing the formal syntax of "State-Action-State Increment," ASD reduces distinct phenomena to Generalized Constitutive Relations that possess a unified structure. This formalization creates a critical bridge between observed phenomena and their mathematical expressions, directly addressing the challenge of incommensurability by providing a common semantic language for models across scientific domains. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through three progressively complex applications. The analysis of Newtonian Mechanics re-interprets inertia as an Internal Action. The study of material constitutive relations validates the use of the Generalized State Parameter to formally model path dependence and system memory in Non-Markovian systems. Finally, the application to soil consolidation illustrates ASD's power in logically integrating multi-scale, multi-mechanism coupled processes. ASD provides a powerful conceptual tool for advancing the goal of scientific methodological unification.

detail.title: From Small to Large: A Graph Convolutional Network Approach for Solving Assortment Optimization Problems
detail.abstract: Assortment optimization seeks to select a subset of substitutable products, subject to constraints, to maximize expected revenue. The problem is NP-hard due to its combinatorial and nonlinear nature and arises frequently in industries such as e-commerce, where platforms must solve thousands of such problems each minute. We propose a graph convolutional network (GCN) framework to efficiently solve constrained assortment optimization problems. Our approach constructs a graph representation of the problem, trains a GCN to learn the mapping from problem parameters to optimal assortments, and develops three inference policies based on the GCN's output. Owing to the GCN's ability to generalize across instance sizes, patterns learned from small-scale samples can be transferred to large-scale problems. Numerical experiments show that a GCN trained on instances with 20 products achieves over 85% of the optimal revenue on problems with up to 2,000 products within seconds, outperforming existing heuristics in both accuracy and efficiency. We further extend the framework to settings with an unknown choice model using transaction data and demonstrate similar performance and scalability.

detail.abstract: The efficiency of Kenya's pension schemes invites elevated interest owing to the increasing pension contribution amounts and the expectation that benefits paid out of these schemes would protect members from old age poverty. The study investigates the intervening effect of risk management on the relationship between corporate governance and the efficiency of pension schemes in Kenya. The study employs panel data consisting of 896 observations from 128 schemes in a sample period from 2015 to 2021. The study finds that risk management significantly mediates the relationship between employee representatives on the board of trustees, as a component of corporate governance, and the efficiency of pension schemes. Consequently, the mediation effect of risk management indicates that when employee representatives are involved in governance, the presence of strong risk management practices ensures that their contributions lead to improved efficiency. Risk management, therefore, serves as a critical safeguard that enables governance structures to function more effectively and contribute to the overall performance of the scheme.

detail.abstract: As life expectancy in Kenya increases, so does the need for efficient pension schemes that can secure a dignified retirement and protect members from oldage poverty. Limited research, however, has explored the efficiency of these schemes under existing governance structures. This study addresses that gap by examining the combined effects of corporate governance, risk management, and industry regulation on pension scheme efficiency in Kenya. Using a quantitative design, we conducted a panel regression analysis on a seven-year secondary dataset of 128 Kenyan pension schemes, totalling 896 observations. Our results reveal significant insights: the presence of employee representatives on the board and effective risk management have a significant positive effect on efficiency. Conversely, independent board members exhibit a significant negative effect. Other factors, including top management representation, female board members, and industry regulation, showed no significant effect on efficiency in the joint model. These findings suggest that the impact of governance and risk management on efficiency is nuanced, with specific factors-like employee representation-playing a more prominent role. We propose that the electoral process for employee board members may introduce a "self-cleaning mechanism" that progressively enhances scheme efficiency. This mechanism offers a novel theoretical extension of Agency Theory, explaining the convergence of interests between elected trustees and scheme members.

A quantitative survey involving 105 lecturers was conducted, and the data were analyzed using structural equation modeling. The findings reveal that both supportive organizational climate and transformational leadership significantly and positively affect job satisfaction and innovative work behavior. Moreover, job satisfaction plays a mediating role, suggesting that a positive work environment and effective leadership enhance lecturer satisfaction, which in turn fosters innovation. These results highlight the strategic importance of building a supportive organizational culture and developing transformational leadership capacity to strengthen innovation and institutional sustainability in higher education. The study also contributes theoretically by validating the Stimulus Organism Response framework in the context of vocational education.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces an original analytical framework D = (M + A) × Cʷ developed by Ertiza Abbas in 2024-2025 to explain long-term strategic outcomes. Dominance (D) is expressed as the product of Mass and Alliances (M + A) multiplied by Cooperation (C) raised to the power of Worldview (W). Eleven major conflicts from 1950-2025 (Korean War through Ukraine and hypothetical Taiwan scenarios) are examined. In every case where conventional material metrics predicted rapid victory, collapse or stalemate occurred precisely when the ostensibly stronger power suffered degradation of internal cohesion (C) and collapse of justifying narrative (W). The exponent proves decisive. The framework offers predictive power superior to traditional realist variables and explains why high-W, high-C actors routinely neutralize 10-50× material disadvantages. The formula is offered as a permanent contribution to strategic studies. Formula for Strategic Dominance: D = (M + A) × C^W, an original framework conceived in 2024-2025. Eleven major conflicts (1950-2025) and one near-future scenario are tested. In every case, collapse or stalemate of the materially superior side occurred exactly when internal cohesion (C) and justifying worldview (W) decayed-rendering even 50:1 advantages irrelevant. The exponent proves decisive. The formula consistently outperforms traditional materialist metrics and is offered as a permanent, predictive contribution to strategic studies. This Research paper is a part of Ertiza Abbas's book "The Establishment".

detail.abstract: This paper is exploring De-employability both as a concept and process using sociological theory of AGIL modelling. With South Africa celebrating more than 30 years of democracy, a lot has been achieved especially in terms of affirmative action particularly racial and gender disparities redressing, even though this view is contested. Women empowerment through social policy is one of the trademarks that make South Africa different from her continental counterparts, over the past 03 decades we have seen female representation in fields that were previously male dominated. Mining, engineering; and general to executive management is evident in this regard. These achievements can be attributed to the conflict school of thought through the feminist frameworks. During apartheid in South Africa, Black South African males were disadvantaged, like other disadvantaged groups and were hoping for improved living conditions. Affirmative action aimed to address past inequalities, but the introduction and implementation of gender-based social policies among Black South Africans are causing a crisis that will require attention in the coming decades. For example, the Employment Equity Act applies to all types of employment, including internships and entry-level jobs, where black male students directly from university are at high risk of unemployment because of policies that prioritise black women over black men. This paper employs a qualitative research systematic review using the analytical realism paradigm. The paper discusses the structural de-employability of Black South African male graduates, arguing that deemployability is a concept rooted in understanding causal mechanisms. The argument is that theoretical models, like Parson's sociological theory, should reflect true causal structures related to the unemployment of these graduates, rather than just simplifying phenomena through models with unrealistic assumptions. This paper integrates analytical realism with grounded theory to offer a precise and abstract sociological concept of de-employability, critiquing instrumentalist approaches for their lack of realism. It contrasts with other scholars who use grounded theory purely as a paradigm, whereas this paper uses it as a research design to produce the new idea of deemployability based on Parson's AGIL model. The academic literature has not yet paid attention to the negative impact of this social policy on the employability of black South African men, despite their qualifications. Findings suggest that the latent function of the gender skewed social policy has failed to deliver the democratic gains for black South African males, the anomie of the same person remains unaccounted for. This study therefore recognises the systematic exclusion of Black South African Males from employment opportunities as De-employability and should be addresses using AGIL sociological model.

detail.title: "The Two Islams" Publication Series: Operationalizing the Distinction: A Policy Framework for Differentiating between Traditional Islam and Political Islamism
detail.abstract: This policy brief addresses a critical failure in contemporary security and immigration policy: the persistent conflation of the religion of Islam with the political ideology of Islamism. This analytical error alienates the vast majority of peaceful Muslims—who are the primary victims of Islamist extremism—and undermines the effectiveness of counter-terrorism efforts. To rectify this, the brief provides a clear, actionable diagnostic toolkit that differentiates Traditional Islam (a personal faith compatible with pluralism and the nation-state) from Political Islamism (a totalitarian ideology seeking to establish a global caliphate). Key differentiators include the primary source of religious authority, the goal of political engagement, and attitudes toward other faiths and local cultures. The brief concludes with concrete policy recommendations for immigration screening, counter-terrorism resource allocation, and community engagement. The central argument is that by precisely targeting the ideology and not the faith, states can split the enemy, build stronger alliances with traditional Muslim communities, and more effectively defend pluralistic societies against a totalitarian threat.

detail.title: How Digital Media Markets Amplify News Sentiment
detail.abstract: This paper examines how digital market incentives shape the emotional tone of news headlines and the transmission of information. An analysis of more than 330,000 newspaper articles demonstrates that online headlines are markedly more emotional and negative than their print counterparts. Experiments with professional journalists show that stronger economic incentives to attract attention causally induce more emotional and negative headline choices. Complementary reader experiments indicate that such attention-driven environments increase engagement, but reduce factual learning. The findings document a market-based mechanism of media bias through which attention incentives amplify emotional framing in headlines and, in turn, impair audience learning.

title: Stakeholder Support and the Effectiveness of Carbon Disclosure Mandate

detail.title: Stakeholder Support and the Effectiveness of Carbon Disclosure Mandate
detail.abstract: We show that stakeholder support plays a critical role in enabling disclosure mandates to achieve effective carbon reduction. Specifically, we examine a 2021 Chinese disclosure mandate intended to incentivize corporate carbon reduction and show that it produces different effects depending on the level of stakeholder support. We define treatment firms as those that undertook emission-reduction efforts in response to the mandate, and control firms as those that did not. We then categorize firms based on the level of institutional support in their headquarter regions, including the availability of carbon management professionals, green financing from local central bank branches, and environmental spending by local governments. We find that only treatment firms in regions with strong stakeholder support significantly reduce carbon intensity and emissions relative to matched control firms. These findings suggest that disclosure regulations alone cannot drive substantive emission reductions, and effective corporate decarbonization requires coordinated support from multiple external stakeholders.

detail.abstract: As climate-related risks become increasingly material to corporate performance and investor decision-making, the need for consistent, comparable disclosure standards has become urgent. Yet efforts to establish a global baseline have been hindered by regulatory fragmentation and competing frameworks. While the European Union's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) was expected to trigger a "Brussels Effect" and define the global norm, its scope has since been scaled back in response to political and economic pressures. The United States had similarly retreated from comprehensive disclosure mandates. Against this backdrop, the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has emerged, somewhat unexpectedly, as the leading platform for global convergence. Created under the authority of the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Foundation, the body responsible for developing globally recognized accounting standards, the ISSB leveraged its institutional credibility and infrastructure to accelerate uptake. This paper argues that the ISSB's success stems not from regulatory power, but from its institutional design and grounding in private-sector practice. Notably, it builds directly on the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), a fully market-driven initiative created by and for private actors to produce financially material, decision-useful disclosures. By integrating SASB and Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)'s risk framework, the ISSB offers a model that is both credible and pragmatic, one already familiar to global capital markets. This paper shows how the ISSB has transformed private standardsetting into a viable global baseline for climate disclosure.

detail.abstract: This study examines the causal impact of additional financial aid granted to students living far from university on their academic performance. It exploits an Italian policy that supports the relocation of scholarship recipients to the university city. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design based on a travel-time eligibility threshold, we compare the academic outcomes of scholarship holders enrolled at a medium-sized public university. Results indicate that relocated students accumulate credits more slowly and achieve lower average grades than comparable commuters, with no evidence that relocated students trade exam quality for quantity. A mediation analysis suggests that these effects may be driven by time-management difficulties and the limited adequacy of the financial support to cover living expenses. By focusing on an overlooked dimension of student aid, the paper contributes to the understanding of how financial support mechanisms interact with students' living arrangements and provides novel causal evidence on the interplay between financial aid and students' living arrangements in higher education.

title: Does Digitalization Lead to Climate Awareness? A Cross-Country Panel Data Analysis
affiliations: Islamic University, Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP), Linkoping University - Department of Management and Engineering Division, Linkoping University - Department of Management and Engineering Division, Asian Development Bank - Economic Research and Asian Development Bank

detail.title: Does Digitalization Lead to Climate Awareness? A Cross-Country Panel Data Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 821

detail.abstract: Climate change, currently one of the most pressing challenges, requires increased public awareness and decisive action to support effective mitigation efforts. Comprehending digitalization’s potential role in shaping public understanding of climate-related issues has become a progressively important area of study. Against this backdrop, we undertake a pioneering attempt to examine how digitalization influences climate change awareness across diverse countries. To capture the multifaceted nature of digitalization, we construct a digitalization index, applying principal component analysis. Leveraging an annual panel dataset encompassing 65 countries over 2005–2020, our study applies several econometric techniques: panel-corrected standard errors, feasible generalized least squares, two-step system generalized method of moments, and panel quantile regression, to investigate this nexus. Our findings unveil a nonlinear U-shaped relationship between digitalization and climate awareness, suggesting that digitalization initially has a negligible or adverse impact but substantially boosts climate awareness after a digital maturity threshold is achieved. Furthermore, the share of renewable energy consumption also follows a U-shaped nonlinear pattern, while household consumption and corruption control contribute to boosting climate awareness. Conversely, the impact of human development, gross fixed capital, and trade openness becomes negligible when endogeneity is controlled. Our quantile-based analysis further validates these conclusions, although some factors vary across quantiles. These findings carry important policy implications, particularly emphasizing targeted fiscal policies to strengthen digital infrastructure and climate communication efforts, thereby facilitating tailored strategies for improved public climate awareness to meet climate sustainability.

detail.title: Rethinking GPR: the sources of geopolitical risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2522

detail.abstract: Geopolitical risks and tensions are nowadays regularly presented by policymakers and analysts as key conditioning factors of economic activity in both the short and the medium-run. Widely accepted operational measures of geopolitical risks tend to be based on counting the number of newspaper articles related to adverse geopolitical events, in particular following the ground-breaking paper of Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) in which they build their Geopolitical Risk (GPR) indexes. In this paper we propose one avenue to make further progress in the measurement of such risks. We provide a decomposition of GPR by exploiting the idea that the geopolitical risks that a country faces can be traced back to the countries or entities that are the source of those risks. In this regard, we exploit the idea that geopolitical risk linked to a specific geography or political entity can be interpreted as a “bilateral GPR”, and that the aggregation of such bilateral GPRs provides a natural way of interpreting the overall GPR index. We show that our indexes add distinct information from the benchmark GPR, and together form a more accurate representation of the geopolitical tensions currently present between the major economies. We also show that the geographical origin of a given GPR shock determines its macroeconomic effect in a given economy (as computed from standard VAR models), both in terms of the intensity of such effect and even its sign (i.e. whether a particular GPR shock causes GDP to increase or decrease).

detail.abstract: This working paper argues that the central ideological conflict of our time is not between "the West and Islam," but between pluralistic civilization and the totalitarian project of Political Islamism. Through a comparative analysis of case studies-including the genocidal campaigns against the Yezidi and Druze peoples, the cultural erasure of the Baluch, and the ideological subversion of Indonesia's Islam Nusantara-this paper traces how Political Islamism weaponizes theology and Arab cultural supremacy to systematically dismantle religious and cultural diversity. It further posits that the international focus on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict functions as a strategic diversion, providing moral camouflage for this broader campaign of ideological purification. The paper concludes with a call for a fundamental reorientation of moral and political resources toward the defense of the world's most vulnerable and ancient communities.

title: From Biodiversity Conservation to Stock Price Stability: International Evidence of Biodiversity Impact Reduction in Mitigating Stock Price Crash Risk

detail.title: From Biodiversity Conservation to Stock Price Stability: International Evidence of Biodiversity Impact Reduction in Mitigating Stock Price Crash Risk
detail.abstract: We examine whether biodiversity conservation reduces future stock price crash risk. Using global data from 41 countries between 2005 and 2022, we demonstrate that firms that take concrete actions to mitigate biodiversity impacts face significantly lower future crash risk. The effect is amplified by strong governance, climate-linked CEO pay, stakeholder-oriented legal regimes, and high national pollution pressure, but attenuated for firms that are opaque, financially constrained, or carbon-intensive. Firm fixed-effects, first-difference models, entropy balancing, and a difference-in-differences design centred on natural-disaster shocks address endogeneity. Mediation tests show that a higher ESG standing and fewer negative environmental news events partially transmit the benefit. By introducing biodiversity as a priced environmental risk, our paper expands the ESG-finance interface and offers new insights into the relationship between ecological stewardship and asset price stability.

title: Executive Clemency and Immigration Federalism: Reconsidering Presidential Power Over Deportation Orders

detail.title: Executive Clemency and Immigration Federalism: Reconsidering Presidential Power Over Deportation Orders

publicationDetails.detailsText: Minnesota Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-51
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Minnesota Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Given the lack of clear historical precedent and the unique nature of deportation’s function in the criminal justice system, this article advocates for a constitutional basis for the President’s authority to grant clemency for deportation orders imposed on lawful permanent residents, refugees, or other noncitizens stripped of their legal immigration status as a result of mandated deportation after a criminal conviction. 

We contend  that violations of the immigration statute that mandate deportation based on criminal convictions are punitive in nature and thus while civil, are nonetheless a penalty; second, we contend that given this punitive nature, violations of such laws qualify as "offenses against the United States" and, therefore, are eligible for clemency under the President's pardon power. Because deportation as a process is completely and exclusively federal, it does not matter whether the underlying crimes that resulted in the deportation orders are state or federal. Deportation is a federal penalty which places it within the ambit of the President’s constitutional power to grant a reprieve under the pardon clause.

title: The Impact of Firm Complexity on Financial Leverage
affiliations: Penn State Harrisburg, Old Dominion University - Strome College of Business and Youngstown State University

detail.title: The Impact of Firm Complexity on Financial Leverage
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of firm complexity on corporate leverage decisions. We find that more complex firms maintain significantly higher market and book leverage.  These results remain robust across alternative specifications and after addressing endogeneity concerns through instrumental variable and propensity score matching approaches. Further analyses reveal that agency costs represent a key mechanism, as institutional monitoring substitutes for debt discipline, whereas excess free cash flow amplifies leverage. Moreover, managerial ability mitigates the positive relation between complexity and leverage, indicating that capable managers rely less on debt as a governance tool. Finally, while both complexity and leverage individually reduce firm value, their interaction alleviates this effect, suggesting that debt is used strategically in complex firms to enhance efficiency.

title: Do Firms Pollute More after Going Public? Evidence from Hydraulic Fracturing Operators

detail.title: Do Firms Pollute More after Going Public? Evidence from Hydraulic Fracturing Operators
detail.abstract: We examine changes in firms’ environmental externality and pollution intensity after going public, using detailed project-level data of hydraulic fracturing (HF) operators. Employing a difference-in-differences design, we find that after their initial public offerings (IPO), the operators use more toxic chemicals per well, compared with non-IPO operators that drill wells in the same period and the same area. Further analysis suggests that the increase in pollution intensity is related to firms’ incentives to maximize short-term profits and the enhanced risk sharing with new shareholders after IPOs. Finally, we find that after the operators go public the concentration of the toxic chemicals increases in surface water near the wells. Our results suggest that going public may exacerbate firms’ negative environmental externality.

title: Assessing Long-term Climate Trends in Central Bangladesh: A Case Study of Tangail District
