title: The Evolution of Macroprudential Policy in Chinese Real Estate Market (2015-2024)

detail.title: The Evolution of Macroprudential Policy in Chinese Real Estate Market (2015-2024)
detail.abstract: Financial stability is a critical component of economic health, with real estate markets often serving as both barometers and catalysts of macroeconomic impulse. From this view, macroprudential policy has been evolving as a key regulatory approach to address systemic risks following the 2008 financial crisis, with particular attention to housing markets due to their procyclicality and strong linkages to financial systems. In emerging economies like China, where real estate accounts for approximately 20% of GDP, understanding the dynamics between sectoral financial conditions and broader economic activity is crucial for effective policy design, yet measuring these relationships has been challenging due to complex interplay and diverse understanding of monetary policy transmission channels and market expectations. The specific challenge this study addresses is the lack of sector-specific financial condition indices capable of capturing the temporal dynamics and causal relationships between real estate financial conditions and broader economic activity in China's unique financial system. Here we show that our constructed Real Estate Financial Condition Index (RE-FCI) demonstrates statistically significant lead-lag and directional causal relationships with the Li Keqiang Index, a proxy for Chinese economic activity. Contrary to conventional wisdom that treats financial condition indices primarily as descriptive tools, our analysis reveals that the RE-FCI serves as a leading indicator of economic activity with a 7-month lead time (correlation = -0.37), while also participating in a feedback loop where economic conditions influence real estate financial conditions with a quarterly delay. The robustness of these causal relationships across multiple analytical frameworks (standard PCMCI, robust PCMCI, and ensemble approaches) validates the RE-FCI's transition from a descriptive metric to a predictive instrument with genuine policy relevance. Our findings provide empirical evidence that sector-specific financial condition monitoring can enhance the precision and timeliness of macroprudential policies, potentially preventing the amplification of economic cycles through real estate markets. These insights contribute to the discourse on Chinese financial stability by demonstrating how advanced analytical techniques can transform sectoral indicators into actionable policy tools, with possible implications extending beyond China to other emerging economies facing similar challenges in managing real estate-driven economic cycles.

title: From Regeneration to Coherence: The Origin of the Planetary Innovation Ecology

detail.title: From Regeneration to Coherence: The Origin of the Planetary Innovation Ecology
detail.abstract:
From Regeneration to Coherence traces the emergence of Planetary Innovation Ecology (PIE) — a new philosophy and science of innovation grounded in Earth’s aliveness. Drawing from lived experimentation across clean technology, distributed manufacturing, and systemic design, the paper explores how humanity’s models of innovation remain largely incremental, confined to anthropocentric paradigms of regeneration and optimization. It argues that the next paradigm demands a transition from regeneration to coherence — a state in which human creativity realigns with the organizing logic of living systems.

While systems thinkers such as Capra and Luisi articulated the living-systems view of life, and Earth-system scientists like Folke and Rockström mapped planetary boundaries, none have treated innovation itself as a living ecological process or proposed ways to measure its alignment with planetary intelligence. Planetary Innovation Ecology fills this gap. It defines innovation as a co-evolutionary phenomenon within the biosphere and introduces two new instruments — the Planetary Coherence Index and the Planetary Symbiosis Index — to assess how human systems evolve toward reciprocal thriving with Earth. Together, these ideas form the groundwork for a new planetary science of innovation — one in which invention becomes participation in the evolutionary intelligence of life itself.

title: The health and economic costs of welfare reform: a quasi-experimental evaluation of the roll-out of Universal Credit in England
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Department of Economics, The University of Manchester - School of Health Sciences, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems, Newcastle University - Population Health Sciences Institute, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems, University of Glasgow - MRC/CSO Social and Public Health Sciences Unit, Lancaster University, Northumbria University, University of Glasgow - Institute of Health and Wellbeing, University of Glasgow - Institute of Health and Wellbeing, University of Liverpool, Newcastle University, University of Essex, University of Liverpool - Department of Public Health, Policy and Systems and The University of Manchester

detail.title: The health and economic costs of welfare reform: a quasi-experimental evaluation of the roll-out of Universal Credit in England
detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on the mental health and care service impacts of the roll-out of Universal Credit, one of the most significant welfare reforms in Europe in recent decades. Designed to simplify benefits and strengthen work incentives by merging six means-tested programmes into a single payment, Universal Credit also introduced stress-inducing features that may harm mental health, including stringent conditionality, sanctions, a five-week wait for the first payment, and greater financial management burdens. Exploiting the plausibly exogenous, staggered geographical introduction of Universal Credit across England (2013-2018), we implement a staggered difference-in-differences framework using comprehensive administrative data from the Small Area Mental Health Index at Lower-layer Super Output Area level. We find substantial adverse effects: a 0.10 SD increase in clinically diagnosed depression prevalence, a 0.03 SD rise in mental health-related hospital admissions and attendances, and a 0.06 SD increase in antidepressant prescribing. In natural units, these correspond to about 113,742 additional depression cases, 29,993 extra hospital admissions and attendances, and 1.29 million more antidepressant prescriptions annually by 2018. Effects are immediate and persistent, larger for areas exposed earlier, and increase with local uptake. Results are robust across specifications, sensitivity analyses, and alternative estimators. Indicative valuations imply sizeable societal and healthcare costs of approximately £2.84 billion annually, indicating important externalities of the reform. These findings underscore the need to incorporate mental health and care service consequences into the design, implementation, and evaluation of welfare policy.

detail.abstract: Digital health services increasingly cross-national borders, yet legal uncertainty persists over how to regulate telemedicine across jurisdictions. In September 2025, the European Court of Justice delivered a landmark ruling on the case ‘DrSmile’ (C-115/24), clarifying the EU Cross-Border Healthcare Directive 2011/24/EU and defining the difference between purely remote and mixed ‘hybrid’ models of telemedicine. The Court held that a provider established in one Member State may deliver telemedical care across the EU under the professional and patient-safety rules of the provider’s country, while any in-person treatment remains governed by the patient’s country law. It further defined telemedicine as care delivered entirely at a distance by electronic means and confirmed that the provider’s country-of-origin rule extends beyond reimbursement; in particular to licensing, oversight, and safety standards. We analyse these rulings in the broader context of EU regulatory fragmentation and cross-border consumer protection, evaluating their implications for patients, telemedicine businesses, traditional practitioners, and public health policymakers. Finally, we consider how this decision could reinforce the importance of international standards for digital health governance and the lessons it offers to the US, UK, and other non-EU countries.

detail.title: Foreign direct investment in Spain in a context of fragmenting international relations
detail.abstract: This article describes the behaviour of Spain's foreign direct investment (FDI) flows and stocks in recent years, against a backdrop in which firms and governments increasingly take into account geostrategic considerations in their decisions on such transactions. Takeaways • Over the past decade, inward FDI flows have performed better in Spain than at global level and in the main euro area economies. • The geographical composition of Spain's stock of inward FDI suggests a relatively low exposure to geopolitical risk, with other European Union countries being the ultimate counterpart for nearly 50% of the country's total FDI stock in 2023. The second most important source of Spain's FDI is the United States, which accounts for 14%. • However, in the current complex setting, extraordinary uncertainty surrounds the stability and strength of some traditional geopolitical alignments.

title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications: Comment
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business and Stanford University

detail.title: The Rise of Market Power and the Macroeconomic Implications: Comment
detail.abstract:
De Loecker et al. (2020) (DEU) estimate that markups increased significantly in the United States from 1955 to 2016. We find this result is sensitive to unreported sample restrictions that drop 27% of the available observations. Applying the methodology as described in the article to the full sample, markup increases are more muted until late in the sample period, and are almost entirely driven by Finance and Insurance firms. If these firms are removed, markup increases are modest. We conclude that the DEU methodology and data, as they are described in the article, do not support the conclusion that broad-based increases in market power have occurred in recent decades.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the potential for sustainable development in the Cumilla region of Bangladesh, driven by its cultural heritage. The analysis centers on two underutilized assets: the region's unique Khadi textile tradition, which has recently received Geographical Indication (GI) status, and its significant archaeological sites. The study argues that these assets, strategically leveraged, can catalyze broad economic revival. To explore this, the research employs a multi-scalar framework that connects micro-level factors, such as artisan capabilities, with macro-level obstacles, including infrastructure gaps and disjointed policy. A pivotal argument is that reviving and modernizing the dormant Cumilla Airport is a necessary precondition for improving regional access. This enhanced connectivity is vital for unlocking high-value export opportunities for Khadi products and for developing heritage tourism, particularly to attract markets within the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The Government of Bangladesh should champion the inclusion of Cumilla's archaeological sites and Khadi heritage in the official tourism promotional material of both SAARC and BIMSTEC as suggested by the author. The study also advances community-driven development strategies, outlining proposals for immersive tourist experiences and targeted skill upgradation programs designed to distribute economic benefits equitably. Ultimately, by merging the goals of cultural preservation with welfare economics, this paper provides specific policy prescriptions to position Cumilla as a benchmark for sustainable, heritagebased development.

title: What if the Long Forward Rate is Flat?
affiliations: Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University

detail.title: What if the Long Forward Rate is Flat?
detail.abstract: This paper draws on the theory of Dybvig, Ingersoll, and Ross (Journal of Business, 1996) to show that long forward rates are constant in asymptotically stationary and ergodic economies, thereby extending the applicability of long-run pricing kernel factorizations developed by Alvarez and Jermann (Econometrica, 2005) and Hansen and Scheinkman (Econometrica, 2009). As a simple application, we identify a limitation of a popular framework for term structure modeling, namely the Markov potential method. This mathematical approach relies on a path-independent pricing kernel, which implicitly restricts the market price of risk to equal the long-term bond volatility. By contrast, the general equilibrium framework of Cox, Ingersoll, and Ross (Econometrica, 1985) is free from this limitation, because its pricing kernel is path-dependent.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines the regulatory treatment of tokenized bank deposits under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation. It shows a comprehensive taxonomy distinguishing tokenized deposits from deposit tokens based on their technical architectures and authentication models, and explores implementation strategies that range from two-layer coexistence models to complete migration architectures.

The research highlights that the EU's decision to exclude tokenized bank deposits from MiCAR's scope—retaining them under traditional banking supervision through the principle of technological neutrality—maintains regulatory coherence but introduces structural limitations. A comparative analysis of non-EU frameworks as well as regulatory developments in the United States and Asia, suggests that other jurisdictions have adopted more proactive strategies to address the operational challenges associated with distributed ledger technology in banking.

The analysis identifies significant gaps at the intersection of regulatory principles and private law, particularly concerning legal status, transferability and settlement finality, insolvency protection, and monetary stability. The study concludes that while technological neutrality is theoretically sound, it necessitates additional legal guidance to clarify the application of traditional private law concepts to blockchain-based banking instruments. In the absence of such guidance, the current framework risks creating operational uncertainty that could hinder innovation and place European institutions at a competitive disadvantage in the rapidly evolving landscape of digital finance.

title: Biodiversity risks and lender credit allocation: The role of lenders' commitments to environmental sustainability
affiliations: Lund University - Department of Economics; Knut Wicksell Centre for Financial Studies, Lund University - Department of Economics, Stockholm University - Stockholm Business School and Stockholm Business School, Stockholm University

detail.title: Biodiversity risks and lender credit allocation: The role of lenders' commitments to environmental sustainability
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how financial institutions incorporate biodiversity risks into lending and loan resale decisions, comparing UNEP FI-committed and non-committed institutions. Using global loan-level data from Reuters DealScan (2010-2023), we analyze how lenders adjust loan size and secondary-market sales in response to firms' biodiversity impact and dependency risks. We find that all lenders treat biodiversity dependency as a financially material risk, extending smaller loans to more biodiversity-dependent firms. By contrast, only committed lenders respond to impact risk by reducing credit to high-impact borrowers and, when industry differences are not controlled for, appearing more likely to offload such exposures in the secondary market. This suggests that resale behavior mainly reflects sectoral variation in biodiversity intensity rather than firm-level risk. Overall, non-committed lenders focus on financial materiality, while committed lenders internalize double materiality by aligning credit allocation and portfolio management with sustainability objectives.

title: International Reserves as a Pillar of BRICS' Stressability amid Global Geopolitical Shocks: the Potential for BRICS and ASEAN Monetary Arrangements

detail.title: International Reserves as a Pillar of BRICS' Stressability amid Global Geopolitical Shocks: the Potential for BRICS and ASEAN Monetary Arrangements
detail.abstract: The BRICS's international reserves (IR), which have long been used for smoothing domestic economic stress, reached today a record level, but external risks exacerbated by global geopolitical shocks. While verifying the nexus between outside driven trade, broad money supply and external debt and dynamics of BRICS's IR we found structural shifts in data series in quadratic regression models after two geopolitical eventsthe Covid-19 in 2020-2022 and Q2 of 2022. E.g. after Q2 2022 the short-term external debt determined Russia's IR twice stronger, the M2 negative influence became weaker and compressed partly due to dedollarization. According to the findings, export revenue became more significant than M2 in controlling domestic demand in Russia and Brazil, and less in India and South Africa. The combination of factors determines the speed of IR recovery after an external shock: for Russia from 6-to 12-month liquidity reserve is needed to mitigate outflows from external trade because of geopolitical shocks, for Brazil 9-month reserve while a median for BRICS is 3-6 month. Thus, stresses of trade and debt variables cointegratively reduce the BRICS' IR, requiring a multiple larger reserve of emergency liquidity. To strengthen the BRICS's monetary capacity to safeguard against global turbulence and economic sanctions BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) may serve. Insofar equipped with such settlements elements as non-common accounts for reserve assets, swap-covered borrowing, universal terms of financing BRICS CRA may expand bilateral swap and repurchase agreement facilities among these countries. Moreover, a single contractual agreement between the BRICS CRA and the Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralization (CMIM) may be considered as a self-help and multilateral support mechanism. We bear similar exchange rate and interest risks, which can be facilitated by lending from specific terms of accesses and use it to cover trade deficit.

title: Four Essays on Short and Long Run Effects of Macroeconomic Volatility
affiliations: Lancaster University - Lancaster University Management School

detail.title: Four Essays on Short and Long Run Effects of Macroeconomic Volatility
detail.abstract: This thesis examines how macroeconomic volatility affects real and nominal dynamics in both the long and short run. The first two chapters show, through a DSGE model and a Bayesian TVP-VAR, that unemployment co-moves positively with low-frequency real and nominal volatility. The third and fourth chapters analyze uncertainty shocks in medium-scale DSGE models, demonstrating that their effects on inflation and output depend crucially on monetary policy persistence. When policy is sufficiently smooth, real uncertainty shocks generate positive inflation responses. Overall, the thesis highlights volatility as a key driver of long-run labor outcomes and short-run macroeconomic fluctuations.

title: The Spillover Effects of Financial Reforms: Evidence from Global Syndicated Loans
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, Renmin University of China - School of Finance, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) - Institute of Chinese Financial Studies (ICFS) and Renmin University of China - School of Finance

detail.title: The Spillover Effects of Financial Reforms: Evidence from Global Syndicated Loans
detail.abstract: This paper examines the cross-border spillover effects of financial reforms through international bank lending. Using detailed syndicated loan data across countries combined with a financial reform index, we identify causal effects of reforms in lending countries on loan pricing and firm performance abroad. Exploiting contemporaneous within-country variation in firms' exposure to foreign lenders, we find that financial reforms in the lending countries significantly lower syndicated loan spreads. The spillovers are more pronounced for firms in developing economies, and translate into higher employment, investment, and sales. The results highlight financial reforms as a distinct channel of international policy transmission.

title: Watchdog or Showdog? Spotlight Chasing in Antitrust Enforcement
affiliations: Yale School of Management and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Watchdog or Showdog? Spotlight Chasing in Antitrust Enforcement
detail.abstract: We study how an acquirer's public visibility affects antitrust enforcement in mergers and its real economic consequences. Using a novel dataset linking FTC and DOJ inspection outcomes to news coverage of merger parties, we exploit within-industry and within-firm variation in visibility under a common political environment. We find that a 10 percent increase in the acquirer's share of industry news coverage raises the likelihood of being flagged by 1.5 to 3 percent. We establish causality using geographical proximity to media outlets as an exogenous source of variation in news coverage. We interpret these results through a political-accountability framework: higher visibility raises the reputational stakes of enforcement, leading regulators to challenge more visible acquirers. Consistent with this accountability framework, the visibility gradient strengthens during congressional appropriations hearings and disappears in lame-duck periods. Finally, visibility-driven scrutiny has real effects: overlooked low-visibility deals gain market power, while flagged acquirers expand inefficiently and face a higher financial burden. Our results highlight how public salience distorts merger review and generates persistent post-merger inefficiencies.

detail.abstract: According to the World Bank, approximately 55 percent of the world's population, 4.2 billion people, live in cities. By 2050, this global urban population is expected to double. This means that almost 7 in 10 people will live in cities. Africa is home to some of the largest and fastest-growing cities in the world, from Cairo in the North to Lagos in the West, Johannesburg in the South, and Nairobi and Dar es Salaam in the East. Given this global outlook on rapid urban growth, what does the future hold for African cities? Instead of replicating Western models of smart cities, which may not fully resonate with the socio-cultural context of African societies, this approach prioritizes locally-driven, culturally-sensitive solutions that prioritize community engagement, indigenous knowledge systems, and local sustainable practices. Framed within African futurism and smart city design principles as approaches to urban planning and environmental management, this paper uses public opinion data to examine the public's perception of the green transition shift in urban development in Africa and the barriers to implementation of smart city design. The study finds that although there is great optimism and futurist thought burgeoning among the public across the African continent, smart city development in Africa is hindered by a complex web of challenges, spanning information and communications technology (ICT) barriers, environmental sustainability concerns, socioeconomic inequalities, and governance inadequacies. These challenges intersect and amplify one another, creating formidable obstacles to the implementation of smart city initiatives across the continent. This study further finds that the public has a set of issues and principles that they think should be leveraged to put futurist thought into action. Leveraging research-based evidence, adopting best practices, and fostering collaboration among stakeholders are viewed as essential for overcoming these barriers and advancing smart city development in Africa. Through integrating technological innovation, environmental sustainability principles, social equity considerations, and streamlining massive green investments along with governance reforms, African cities can perhaps overcome these hurdles to create more technologically advanced, inclusive, sustainable, and resilient cities for the future.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Santa Clara Univ. Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Santa Clara University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Patent Assertion Entities (PAEs) are often viewed as taxing innovative activity; we show how fee shifting in patent litigation can effectively deter their more frivolous assertions, increasing exposed firms' R&D, innovation output, and startup success. Our identification relies on the U.S. Supreme Court's 2014 ruling in Octane Fitness v. ICON Health & Fitness, which broadened courts' discretion to award attorneys fees against exceptionally weak infringement claims. Using a quasi-regression discontinuity design comparing cases pending at Octane's release with those filed and decided before or after, we find that the decision increased defendants' willingness to contest weak claims and prompted plaintiffs, especially PAEs, to file stronger ones. Pending cases saw more fee awards and lower settlement as well as plaintiff success rates; subsequent PAE cases involved stronger patents and higher success rates. A difference-indifferences analysis further shows that Octane boosted innovation: public firms that were particularly exposed to PAE assertions prior to Octane increased R&D and patenting in response, and private startup firms performed better in venture capital markets.

title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Deglobalisation
affiliations: European Union - JRC-Ispra, European Commision, European Commission - Joint Research Center, European Union - European Commission and European University Institute - Economics Department (ECO)

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Deglobalisation
detail.abstract: This paper assesses the macroeconomic impact of deglobalisation scenarios using an estimated three-region global dynamic general equilibrium framework, considering the euro area, the US, and the rest of the world. We focus on two structural deglobalisation trend scenarios: first, exogenous disruptions to inter-regional trade, and second, greater inward orientation that is reflected in a higher home bias. Our simulations reveal that the trade compression caused by deglobalisation significantly reduces economic activity globally and in the individual blocs. Transition dynamics are typically stagflationary and are often characterised by substantial exchange rate fluctuations. We show that bilateral trade disruptions have both direct and indirect effects, which intensify the more regions are open and integrated into global value chains. Additionally, we find that inward orientation is generally costly when occurring universally. However, a unilateral increase in a region’s home bias that entails no other costs, might spur economic activity in the region implementing it. This benefit is at a disproportionate expense to others, as their export markets contract and their currencies devalue. However, if the preference shift entails efficiency costs, in terms of stifled competition or more rigid labour markets, a favourable unilateral outcome is less likely to materialise. Finally, we discuss the international transmission of shocks and show that in a less globalised steady state, external shocks produce less volatility for the euro area economy in terms of GDP and inflation, but there is also less external attenuation of domestic shocks. One implication is that certain structural trends observed in recent decades, such as the ‘globalisation of inflation’, may weaken as a result.
